title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: earlier in E555 Euler applies Lagrange-type interpolation to the sines of an arithmetic progression of arcs nΦ, (n+1)Φ, ... and obtains, for |Φ| suitably restricted, an identity of the form
  Φ·B = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k C(2n+k−1,k) sin((n+k)Φ)/(n+k)^2,  with B = ∫_0^1 x^n(1−x)^{n−1}dx = B(n+1,n).
Scholion 2 (previous page) took Φ = π and Φ = 2π. There Euler noticed the paradox that Φ = 2π gives a wrong quotient, so he keeps only Φ = π. He then sums that series by a double integral.

§24 (this page) takes Φ = π/2. The values sin((n+k)π/2) cycle through sin(nπ/2), cos(nπ/2), −sin(nπ/2), −cos(nπ/2). The series therefore splits into an even part and an odd part:
  (π/2)B = sin(nπ/2)·Σ_j (−1)^j C(2n+2j−1,2j)/(n+2j)^2 − cos(nπ/2)·Σ_j (−1)^j C(2n+2j,2j+1)/(n+2j+1)^2.

The method of Scholion 2 is then reused. Insert powers t^{n+k}, apply (t d/dt)^2 twice, and recognise the binomial series. The even part gives Re(1+it)^{−2n} = [(1+it)^{−2n}+(1−it)^{−2n}]/2. The odd part should be [(1−it)^{−2n}−(1+it)^{−2n}]/(2i). This produces a combination of double integrals ∫dt/t ∫ t^{n−1}(1±it)^{−2n}dt, to be evaluated at t = 1.

To remove the imaginaries Euler sets t = tan ω. Then:
- dt/t = dω/(sin ω cos ω),
- t^{n−1}dt = sin^{n−1}ω dω / cos^{n+1}ω,
- (1±it)^{−2n} = cos^{2n}ω (cos 2nω ∓ i sin 2nω) (de Moivre).
The imaginary parts cancel, and with sin ω cos ω = ½ sin 2ω and θ = 2ω the result is a real double integral:
  (π/2)B(n+1,n) = 2^{−n} ∫_0^{π/2} dθ/sin θ ∫_0^θ sin^{n−1}φ · sin n(π/2 ± φ) dφ.
The upper limit θ = π/2 corresponds to ω = 45°, t = 1.

The purpose is a new 'comparison' of a Beta integral with an iterated trigonometric integral. It continues the remark at the end of §23 that such comparisons are not found among those previously obtained.

The series themselves diverge for n ≥ 3/2, since the binomial coefficients grow like k^{2n−1}. So the identities are to be read as Abel sums or analytic continuations, which the integral form supplies.

§25 then starts Exemplum 3: arcs forming an 'interrupted' arithmetic progression mΦ, nΦ, (1+m)Φ, (1+n)Φ, ...
errors: Sign error in the odd-part identity. Euler writes 2nt − ... = [(1+t√−1)^{−2n} − (1−t√−1)^{−2n}]/(2√−1). Since (1+it)^{−2n} = 1 − 2nit + ..., the right side begins −2nt. The correct identity is [(1−it)^{−2n} − (1+it)^{−2n}]/(2i).

The sign error propagates. The 'hincque colligitur' line carries the wrong signs on the cos(nπ/2) terms, and the final contracted formula has sin(nπ/2 + 2nω), i.e. sin n(π/2 + θ). The correct form is sin(nπ/2 − 2nω), i.e. sin n(π/2 − θ).
Check n = 1: both versions give π/4 = (π/2)·B(2,1), so this case cannot detect the error.
Check n = 2: B(3,2) = 1/12, so the left side is π/24. Euler's printed formula gives (1/4)∫_0^{π/2} dθ/sinθ ∫_0^θ sinφ sin(π+2φ)dφ = −π/24. The corrected sin(π−2φ) version gives +π/24.

Validity gap: the trigonometric series obtained from Φ = π/2 diverge for n ≥ 3/2. Euler silently uses the t→1 limit (Abel summation) without comment, although on the previous page he himself showed the general formula is not valid for all Φ.
Minor: the last line reads 't = cos. ω = 1'; it should be t = tang. ω = 1 at ω = 45°. This is either a misprint or a misreading of the scan.

ideas.what: Splitting the interpolation series at Φ = π/2 into even/odd parts and summing each via the binomial series (1±it)^{−2n} with t ↦ (t d/dt)^{−2} smoothing
ideas.modern_name: Real/imaginary parts of the binomial series; generating-function summation of a 3F2-type series at argument ±i
ideas.where_published: Same technique as §23 of E555 (previous page); widespread in Euler's work

ideas.what: Substitution t = tan ω with de Moivre to eliminate imaginaries: (1+it)^{−2n} = cos^{2n}ω·e^{−2niω}
ideas.where_published: Many Euler papers on integrals with imaginary parameters

ideas.what: Iterated-integral representation of the Beta function: (π/2)B(n+1,n) = 2^{−n}∫_0^{π/2} dθ/sinθ ∫_0^θ sin^{n−1}φ sin n(π/2 − φ) dφ (corrected sign)
ideas.modern_name: Double-integral representation of B(n+1,n) = Γ(n)Γ(n+1)/Γ(2n+1); value of a 3F2 at argument i via analytic continuation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Not a standard named formula; unsure
ideas.where_published: E555 (Opuscula analytica I, 1783); Opera omnia editors may comment on it, unsure

missed.claim: The final trigonometric double-integral identity for the Beta function carries a sign error inherited from the odd-part binomial formula. The correct kernel is sin n(π/2 − θ), not sin n(π/2 + θ); the printed version fails at n = 2. I do not know whether the Opera omnia editors flagged it.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical/editorial interest. Anyone citing this representation should use the corrected sign.

missed.claim: The page derives, from divergent interpolation series, a representation of B(n+1,n) by an iterated trigonometric integral. Euler never verifies it independently, and he does not discuss the divergence of the series for n ≥ 3/2. It is in effect an early use of Abel summation to produce a hypergeometric (3F2 at argument ±i) evaluation.
missed.quote: vbi post integrationem statui oportet θ = 90° = π/2
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a minor curiosity: a closed-form evaluation of a 3F2-type sum at a complex argument, obtained via summation of divergent series. It is likely subsumed by modern hypergeometric theory.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is routine Eulerian manipulation (binomial series, tan substitution, de Moivre) yielding an obscure but not deep integral identity. Its main notable feature is an uncorrected sign error that makes the final printed formula false for n = 2.
transcription_corrections: In the first displayed equation the right side begins '= sin. nπ/2 (1/nn − ...)'. There is no factor 1/2[?] before sin. nπ/2.
The final line likely should read 't = tang. ω = 1' rather than 't = cos. ω = 1'. This could be a misprint in the original or a misreading of the scan.
The odd-series binomial identity is transcribed faithfully but is mathematically mis-signed in the original (see errors).
